art.short:
Good morning, Yamuna. Here is your art briefing for the last two days, with a good deal happening close to home, a neat link to a Booker-winning novel, and some wonderful stories told through objects and faces.

Let me start in Grenoble, where there is something on at the Musée de Grenoble today. This lunchtime, Thursday the fifth, at half past twelve, the museum hosts a concert called Ballade Européenne, with an Irish programme, as part of its Musée en musique series. The listing mentions classical and folk music, so it sounds like a pleasant midday break if you are able to get down from Les Adrets. On Saturday the seventh, at half past two in the afternoon, the museum also has an event called Le dernier passage, open to all audiences. The listing gives very little detail, so I cannot tell you what it is about, but the title is intriguing enough that it may be worth a look at the museum's own programme.

The museum is also showing sculptures and paintings by the American artist Anne Truitt. The listing in the jds.fr site is very short and gives no dates, so do check before you go, but it is at the museum you would most want to visit anyway. Also on Saturday, Le Mois de la Photo has an event at the Ancien musée de Peinture in Grenoble. Again the details are thin, but it is timely and very much on your doorstep.

For something outdoors, the comics artist Jean-Marc Rochette has painted seven new torn-out eyes on a mural in Grenoble, as reported by mesinfos. It is street art by a well-known creator, and the image of those torn-out eyes is striking enough to be worth seeking out on a walk through town.

Now to Lyon, where Le Petit Bulletin has a feature on a comic book about women drivers, nurses and rescuers in military emergency units. It is linked to an exhibition at the CHRD, the Lyon history centre, and it centres on the military doctor Madeleine Pauliac. One of the people interviewed calls it a blind spot of history, and the book sets out to recover that neglected chapter through a graphic narrative. It is exactly the sort of history told through story that you tend to like.

On the literary front, BBC Radio 4's Front Row has a forty-two-minute episode about Orbiting Orbital, a composition by the musician Nitin Sawhney, inspired by Samantha Harvey's Booker-winning novel Orbital. Harvey has written new material for the piece, so it is a lovely case of a novel travelling into music. The same programme touches on a biography of Michael Gambon and an exhibition called Nue Black Aesthetic at the Design Museum.

Several of today's stories are about history held in objects. At the château de Chantilly, Beaux Arts Magazine reports on an exhibition exploring a pink diamond that was stolen in 1926, later recovered and wrapped in legend ever since. The magazine calls it a miracle survivor, and the tale of theft, rediscovery and mystery reads rather like a novel. In London, The Guardian gives a rapturous review to the V&A's exhibition Constantinople to Istanbul, which brings together Byzantine and Ottoman treasures from one great city. The reviewer calls it a lavish celebration of double imperial splendour, and says you will not want to leave. And on a humbler scale, The Guardian also looks at a new exhibition on Roman Scotland, drawn from finds such as altars to the sun god Sol and surviving leather shoes, including a discovery at Inveresk near Edinburgh. Heated floors, flashy sandals and a great many nails: empire in everyday detail.

Then there are portraits, and the question of how a person is made into an image. The National Gallery has put out a short video in which Megan Renoir, great-great-granddaughter of Pierre-Auguste Renoir, talks behind the scenes about the exhibition Renoir and Love. She offers a personal angle on the painter's way of living in the moment. On Front Row again, the artist Sam Taylor-Johnson talks about portraiture and selfhood as her new monograph appears, and the discussion of how portraits are made is a good one. The same episode features the film-maker Sian Heder on Being Heumann and the Disability Rights Movement.

The Guardian, meanwhile, has two pieces on the theme. The South African artist Remofiloe Nomandla Mayisela discusses her playful self-portraits in the Lipservice series. She says she learned early what she was meant to become: a wife, a cook, a keeper of the home. Her character Mrs Martha May, along with the links to shweshwe fabric, is a vivid creation, and you may find her a fine fictional figure to think about. The paper also has a photo essay on the shortlist for the Winston Taylor Photo Portrait Prize 2026, with cowboys, a transgender storm chaser and other striking sitters. It is best enjoyed simply by looking.

Last, a thought about authorship. The Guardian rounds up four free exhibitions, among them Sturtevant's forgeries of Warhol, which test your eye for real against fake, and Cady Noland's sharp critique of American culture. Warhol and the question of who really made a work make for a good conversation with older pupils, perhaps even for your terminale students.

That is all for today, Yamuna, and I hope the Irish music, or at least a good cup of tea, finds you at lunchtime.
art.long:
Good morning, Yamuna. Today's art news begins close to home in Grenoble, then goes to Lyon, and from there to portraits, palaces and a few good stories along the way.

Let me start with the museum, since several things are happening there. Jds.fr lists an exhibition of sculptures and paintings by Anne Truitt at the Musée de Grenoble. I'll be honest that the listing is very short, with no dates and no further detail, so I can't tell you how long it runs or what exactly is on the walls. But it is at the museum you would most want to visit, so it is worth a quick look at the museum's own site before you plan a trip down the valley. A show that pairs sculpture and painting by one artist is often a quiet pleasure, the sort where you move slowly and let the rooms speak to each other.

The museum also has two events close together. Today, Thursday the fifth of November, at half past twelve, there is a lunchtime concert called Ballade Européenne, with an Irish programme. It belongs to the museum's Musée en musique series, and the listing mentions both classical and folk music. If you happen to be in Grenoble at midday, it sounds like a very pleasant way to spend a break, and an Irish programme should have plenty of song and story in it. Then on Saturday the seventh, at half past two, the museum holds an event called Le dernier passage, open to all audiences. The listing gives almost nothing else, so its focus is unclear from the text alone. The title is certainly intriguing, and I would not guess further, but it might be worth a phone call or a glance at the website if Saturday afternoon is free.

Saturday the seventh also brings something for photography lovers. Unidivers lists an event at the Ancien musée de Peinture in Grenoble as part of Le Mois de la Photo. Again the details are thin, but the date and the venue are clear, and it is the sort of thing that is easy to fit into a Saturday in town, perhaps alongside the museum event if they suit one another.

Out on the streets, Mesinfos reports that the comics artist Jean-Marc Rochette has painted seven new torn-out eyes on a mural in Grenoble. It is local street art by a well-known creator, and the idea is striking: eyes that have been torn out, painted large on a wall that the whole city walks past. There is something almost literary about it, a motif that makes you ask who is looking, and who has been blinded. If you are in town, it is worth seeing in person rather than in a photograph, because murals change with the light and with the buildings around them.

Now to Lyon, where Le Petit Bulletin Grenoble, in a piece dated the fourth of November, has a feature on a comic book that tells a neglected chapter of history. The book follows women drivers, nurses and rescuers in military emergency units, and it centres on a military doctor, Madeleine Pauliac. It is linked to an exhibition at the CHRD, the Lyon history centre. The article quotes the phrase that they are telling a blind spot of history, an angle mort, which is a lovely way to put it. I think this one may appeal to you particularly, because it is history recovered through a graphic narrative: you meet the past through characters and their work rather than through dates and treaties. It could also be a gentle bridge for students who find a long historical text daunting but will happily follow a story told in images.

Let me turn to the places where art meets literature, which I know is your favourite ground. On BBC Radio 4's Front Row there is a forty-two minute episode about Orbiting Orbital. This is a composition by the musician Nitin Sawhney, inspired by Samantha Harvey's Booker-winning novel Orbital, and it includes new writing by Harvey herself. So you have a novel becoming music, and then the novelist returning to write again in response. That is a fascinating chain of transformation, and the kind of conversation where you hear how prose with a musical quality can be translated into actual music. The same episode also covers a biography of Michael Gambon and the Nue Black Aesthetic exhibition at the Design Museum, so there is variety if you listen to the whole programme.

And from Chantilly, Beaux Arts Magazine reports on the château's exploration of the pink diamond, with the headline calling it a miracle survivor. The stone was stolen in nineteen twenty-six, later recovered, and has been wrapped in legend ever since. Theft, rediscovery and mystery: it reads like a novel, and I suspect you could build a whole short story, or a lesson on unreliable narration, out of a jewel whose history is told in so many versions. If a trip to Chantilly is ever on the cards, this seems to be a show that treats the object as a character.

Next, two pieces from The Guardian that teach history through objects. The first is a rapturous review of the V&A's exhibition in London, Constantinople to Istanbul, which the critic describes as a lavish celebration of double imperial splendour. It brings together Byzantine and Ottoman treasures from one great city, so you see how a single place carried two empires, one after the other. It is not local, of course, but the review is a pleasure to read for the sense of a city layered like a palimpsest, which is a very novelistic idea. The second is a piece about a new exhibition on Roman Scotland, which asks what the Romans ever gave Scotland. The answers include heated floors, flashy sandals, altars to the sun god Sol, and a great many nails. Among the finds are surviving leather shoes, including a discovery at Inveresk near Edinburgh. I like this because a shoe is such a human object. Someone wore it, walked in it, and lost it, and a thousand years of history suddenly becomes personal. It is the same trick that good historical fiction performs.

That leads naturally to the largest theme today, which is portraits and the question of who a person is allowed to be. The Guardian's Women behind the lens series features the South African artist Remofiloe Nomandla Mayisela, who discusses her playful self-portraits from the Lipservice series. The quote that headlines the piece is striking: she learned early what she was meant to become, a wife, a cook, a keeper of the home. Her pictures question those expected roles, and she plays a character called Mrs Martha May. There are also links to shweshwe fabric, which gives the images texture and a sense of place. For someone who loves strong characters, Mrs Martha May sounds like a figure you could discuss with a class: a persona invented by an artist in order to push back against the persona imposed on her.

On the same theme, Front Row has another episode in which the artist Sam Taylor-Johnson talks about portraiture and selfhood, as a new monograph of her work appears. The discussion of how portraits are made, and what a portrait does to the person in it, is strong material for anyone who thinks about the relationship between a painted or photographed face and a written character. The same programme also features the film-maker Sian Heder, who discusses Being Heumann and the Disability Rights Movement.

Staying with faces, The Guardian has a photo essay on the shortlisted images for the Winston Taylor Photo Portrait Prize for twenty twenty-six. It includes cowboys, a transgender storm chaser and other striking sitters. It is a lively selection and best enjoyed simply by looking, one image at a time, and asking what story each person seems to be telling. It might even work as a writing prompt: choose a portrait and give the sitter a voice.

There is also a short video from the National Gallery, which is worth a few minutes. Megan Renoir, great-great-granddaughter of Pierre-Auguste Renoir, talks behind the scenes about the blockbuster exhibition Renoir and Love. It gives a personal angle on the painter's way of living in the moment, and there is something nice about hearing a descendant speak about an artist who is usually presented only through his canvases. It makes the painter feel like a family story rather than a name on a wall.

Finally, a Guardian roundup of four free exhibitions, which includes two artists with sharp ideas. Sturtevant made forgeries of Warhol, and the show tests the viewer's eye for real versus fake, so you are invited to ask what authorship even means. Cady Noland, meanwhile, offers a pointed critique of American culture. I find the Warhol question particularly rich, because it echoes an old literary puzzle: if someone copies a style perfectly, who is the author? It would make a good conversation with older students, perhaps alongside a discussion of pastiche and parody in fiction.

So, to sum up, if you want something for today, the Irish lunchtime concert at the Musée de Grenoble is the one to catch. For the weekend, keep Saturday the seventh in mind for the museum event and Le Mois de la Photo. And for the quiet evening, the Orbiting Orbital episode and the pink diamond story are both there waiting for you.

Enjoy your day, Yamuna, and may it be full of good light and better stories.

literature.short:
Good morning, Yamuna. Today's literary news has a fine mix of prizes, big storytellers and thoughtful writing about teaching, with a few unexpected stories about books and the lives behind them.

Let me begin with the prizes. The poet Grace Nichols, Guyana-born and British-based, has won the ten thousand pound Royal Society of Literature Pioneer prize, which honours women writers over sixty who broke barriers. The Guardian quotes her described as a trailblazer in the truest sense. She is best known for I Is a Long-Memoried Woman, and it is lovely to see that work recognised again.

At the other end of the scale, China Miéville has won the ten thousand pound Goldsmiths prize for The Rouse. It runs to one thousand two hundred and sixty-four pages, and blends a paranormal thriller with a historical saga across British imperial and Cold War history. The Guardian reports that it took him two decades to write, and the judges called it exuberant and overflowing. One of them said he was destined for this award. Meanwhile RNZ has gathered six experts to give their verdicts on the nominees for the 2026 Booker Prize, if you want critical opinions to set against your own reading.

Now to novels and the pleasures of being carried along by a voice. The Guardian reviews Min Jin Lee's American Hagwon, the third book in her Diaspora Quartet and a follow-up to Pachinko. It follows a Korean family whose devotion to their children's education drives the story, and the reviewer calls it gloriously immersive, with storytelling led by character. If you enjoyed the sweep of Pachinko, this sounds like a natural next step.

The Guardian also asks a wonderful question: was one of the great novels of the Enlightenment written by a man who thought he was a werewolf? It concerns Jan Potocki and The Manuscript Found in Saragossa, a surreal, wandering novel with a famously strange origin story. There is now an exhibition on it, and the curators argue that its global humanism feels relevant today. With such an unreliable, roaming narrator, it seems a book made for lovers of storytelling.

On the subject of form, The Spectator has a piece in which Ben Okri reflects on the power of the short novel. I only have the headline, but Okri on what a small book can do is a promising pairing. And Literary Hub offers an opening passage of fiction called Remember the Bees. It is set on red earth beneath an early, lingering heat, with a grandfather at its centre. It is brief, but it is quiet and sensory, the sort of writing you can step straight into.

Next, writers as teachers, which I thought you might enjoy. Literary Hub carries Natasha Trethewey's remarks from the Harper's Magazine Awards, where John Edgar Wideman received the Lewis H. Lapham Award. She talks about what his writing and teaching offer other writers. Also from Literary Hub, Hanif Abdurraqib writes about teaching high school writers in Columbus, Ohio, and about what he has learned from the poet June Jordan. It is an essay on poetry, teaching and how writers are made, and I suspect it will feel familiar to anyone who stands in front of a class.

Staying with language, there is a letter-style essay on what it means to be a literary translator today. It is addressed to a correspondent named Miranda and built around the untranslatable nature of idioms. The title speaks of building a community of imposters, which is a rather charming way to describe translators.

Then there are the essays on how books relate to life and history. Literary Hub looks at Olivia Manning, the British novelist who died in 1980. She drew lightly on real people in her fiction, and she carried grudges about her reputation. The essay is titled Please Don't Put in the Novel That I Died, which tells you something of her humour. It is a good study of where life ends and the novel begins.

From fiction to history, there is a profile of Erika Mann. In August nineteen forty-five she drove through the night to meet some of the most wanted Nazi war criminals before their prosecution. It is history seen through a journalist's eyes, and it has the tension of a thriller.

History comes in again with an essay on Alan Moore's V for Vendetta as a dystopia for our times. It opens in the medieval undercroft beneath the Palace of Westminster, which is a striking place to begin.

Two last pieces have a gentler, more bookish spirit. One is an essay on the olfactory history of book collecting. It begins with Richard de Bury's Philobiblion of thirteen forty-five, in which he praised Paris booksellers as more aromatic than spicery. Next time you open a secondhand book at a flea market, you may think of him. The other is Ry Herman on finding inspiration in queer fairytales. Herman describes searching for old stories with LGBTQ+ subtext, and finding reassurance that queer people have always been present in them. It joins folklore and literature in a thoughtful way.

That is everything for today, and I hope some quiet moment lets you enjoy a few of these with a hot drink.
literature.long:
Good morning, Yamuna. It's a rich couple of days in the literary world, with prizes for a poet and a very large novel, a few stories worth stepping into, and a good run of essays about how writers are made.

Let me begin with the prizes, because two of them are the kind of news you like. The first is for the poet Grace Nichols, who has won the ten thousand pound Pioneer prize from the Royal Society of Literature. The prize honours women writers over sixty who broke barriers, and The Guardian quotes someone calling her a trailblazer in the truest sense. Nichols was born in Guyana and is based in Britain, and she is best known for I Is a Long-Memoried Woman. That title does a great deal of work in very few words. The grammar of it, that defiant, musical "I Is", carries a whole history of voice and memory before you've read a line. If you ever want a short poem to put in front of a class to talk about how language can hold a history, she is a lovely place to start.

The second is rather different in scale. China Miéville has won the ten thousand pound Goldsmiths prize for The Rouse, and the novel is enormous: The Guardian puts it at one thousand, two hundred and sixty-four pages. It blends a paranormal thriller with a historical saga, and it moves across British imperial history and the Cold War. The judges called it exuberant and overflowing, and it apparently took him twenty years to write. One of the quotes in the piece says he was destined for this award. I rather like that a prize built around fiction that breaks the mould has gone to a book that seems to refuse to be tidy. I can't promise it is a novel for a quiet weekend, but a thriller that doubles as a history of empire does sound like something that might suit you.

And a note on the Booker. RNZ has gathered six experts to review the nominees for the twenty twenty-six prize, giving their critical verdicts on the novels in contention. The piece I have is a summary rather than the full text, so I can't tell you what the experts concluded. But if you are following the prize closely, it looks like a useful place to hear several voices disagree.

Now to the stories themselves, starting with one you may want to read on a slower evening. The Guardian reviews American Hagwon by Min Jin Lee, which is the third book in her Diaspora Quartet and a follow-up to Pachinko. It follows a Korean family whose devotion to their children's education drives the story. The reviewer calls it gloriously immersive and praises the character-led storytelling. For a teacher, that premise is almost poignant. The hagwon is the after-school academy, and a novel in which a family sacrifices so much for schooling is bound to resonate with someone who spends her days in a classroom. And it is exactly the sort of book you enjoy: you don't need to know the culture first, because the characters carry you in. If you read Pachinko and liked how it taught history through a family rather than through dates, this seems to continue that tradition.

Then there is something stranger and older. The Guardian has a piece on an exhibition about Jan Potocki and his novel The Manuscript Found in Saragossa. It is a surreal Enlightenment novel with a famously odd origin story, and the headline asks whether one of the great novels of the Enlightenment was written by a man who thought he was a werewolf. The curators argue that the book's global humanism feels relevant now. What I find appealing, and I think you will too, is the narrator: unreliable, wandering, passing from tale to tale, the sort of storyteller who makes you suspect that the story itself is the real protagonist. It is a book that sounds made for readers who love a voice that leads them somewhere and then slips away. It would also sit very well beside an eighteenth-century unit, as a reminder that the Enlightenment had its dreamers and its strangeness as well as its reason.

Staying with the pleasures of form, The Spectator has a piece in which Ben Okri reflects on the power of the short novel, on what that compact form can achieve. I only have the headline and the source, so I can't report what he argues. But Okri is a writer whose prose is so musical that anything he says about craft is worth a look, and the question of what a short book can do that a long one cannot is one that every teacher of fiction ends up asking. It may even be a nice counterweight to the twelve hundred pages of Miéville.

And from Literary Hub there is the opening passage of a piece of fiction called Remember the Bees. It is brief, but it sets its scene beautifully: red earth, an early heat that lingers, and a grandfather at the centre. The narration is sensory and quiet, and it is the kind of opening that works by atmosphere rather than plot. If you collect short passages to read aloud to a class, to show how a writer builds a place from heat and soil and a single figure, this might be one to keep.

Now to a group of pieces about the lives behind books, and about history. Literary Hub has an essay on Olivia Manning, the British novelist who died in nineteen eighty. The title is a line I rather love: Please Don't Put in the Novel That I Died. The essay looks at how Manning drew lightly on real people in her fiction, and how she carried grudges about her own reputation. It is a good look at that eternal question of where life ends and the novel begins, and what it costs the people who get written down. It might make a good prompt for students too, who often ask whether a character is "really" someone the author knew.

On the history side, Literary Hub also has a profile of Erika Mann, the pioneering journalist who, in August nineteen forty-five, drove through the night to meet some of the most wanted Nazi war criminals before they were prosecuted. It is history told through a journalist's eyes, and the image of that night drive is already half a scene from a novel. It is a reminder that reportage and fiction can share a pulse.

There is also an essay on Alan Moore's V for Vendetta as a dystopia for our times. It opens, rather wonderfully, in the medieval undercroft beneath the Palace of Westminster, which is an inspired way to start an argument about a graphic novel that is so concerned with power, memory and the British state. It should interest you for how it treats a text as both craft and history.

And one for the lover of old books. Another Literary Hub essay, The Olfactory History of Book Collecting, begins with Richard de Bury's Philobiblion of thirteen forty-five, in which he praised the booksellers of Paris as more aromatic than spicery. That is a delicious phrase, and it reminds you that people were rhapsodising about the smell of books almost seven hundred years ago. The essay looks at the smells of old books and the history of collecting them. If you spend any time at flea markets, rummaging through boxes of secondhand paperbacks, you will recognise the pleasure at once.

The last group of pieces is about teaching, and about the people who make writers. I think these may be the ones closest to your day job.

Natasha Trethewey has given remarks at the Harper's Magazine Awards, where John Edgar Wideman received the Lewis H. Lapham Award. The transcript is about what Wideman's writing and teaching offer to other writers. It is one thing to be admired for your books, and another to be thanked for what you gave to the people who learned from you, and this speech seems to sit in that second space.

In a similar spirit, the poet Hanif Abdurraqib writes about teaching high school writers in Columbus, Ohio, and what he learned from the poet June Jordan. It is an essay about poetry, teaching, and how writers are made. Teenagers and poetry is exactly your territory, so I imagine you will find him a kindred spirit.

Ry Herman, meanwhile, describes the search for fairy tales with queer subtext, and the reassurance of finding that queer people have always been present in old stories. It is a gentle piece that ties folklore to a contemporary concern, and it is a useful reminder that the old tales are more spacious than the versions we are usually handed. I can see it opening up a good conversation in a class studying fairy tale retellings.

And finally, a letter-style essay on what it means to be a literary translator today. It is addressed to a correspondent named Miranda and built on the untranslatable nature of idioms. For someone who lives between English and French, teaching one literature to students who think in two languages, that idea will probably ring true. The title speaks of building a community of imposters, which is such an honest way to describe a craft that is always about carrying something across without quite managing to.

So that is the shape of it today: a poet honoured for opening doors, a giant novel awarded for refusing to be small, and a long line of teachers and writers reminding us how stories pass from one person to the next. I hope something here follows you into the day.

Enjoy the reading, Yamuna, and may there be a good book waiting for you this evening.

bfi.short:
Good morning, Yamuna. It's a quieter couple of days for official BFI news, but the stage has been busy with the 2027 titles, and a few other pieces might brighten a Thursday.

Hamlet dominates, as it so often does. The Barbican in London has a production called Hamlet: Hail to the Thief, which Country and Town House covers in a stage note. All I have is the headline, so I can't tell you how the production treats the play, but the title suggests a sharp political angle on the usurping king. Further afield, TheUnion.com reports that the Nevada Theatre is presenting what it calls a Hamlet for our time, running through the eighth of November. That is only a few days away, and it is in America, so it is more a curiosity than a plan. Still, the phrase is a handy prompt for première classes: what would it mean to make this play speak to the present, and which lines would a director lean on? BroadwayWorld also announces that Thinking Cap Theatre is presenting Hamlet, though without dates or details in what I have. Three Hamlets in two days, in three different places, is a pleasing reminder of how adaptable the play is. Put side by side, even only as headlines, they could start a good discussion about interpretation.

Two other titles from the 2027 list have turned up on stage. The southlondon.co.uk site reviews Great Expectations at the Brockley Jack Studio in London. I only have the title, so I can't say how the staging handles Pip's voice or the marshes, but it's the sort of review worth reading if you are looking for ideas on bringing the novel to life with seconde or première. Then Patch reports that tickets are on sale for Chatham High School's production of Twelfth Night. There is no date or venue in my information, but it is a nice small sign of Shakespeare being performed by young people, which is rather the spirit of the BFI.

If you enjoy theatre that is brand new, Shakespeare's Globe has a video about its forthcoming play, The Animals Come to the Table, by Timberlake Wertenbaker. It runs at the Sam Wanamaker Playhouse from the eleventh of December to the twenty-fourth of January. In the video, Wertenbaker talks about the work with the director, Anthony Lau. It isn't on the programme, but a short conversation between a playwright and a director is often useful to show a class, as it makes the point that texts are made by people with choices to defend.

On the oral themes, there are two items. The Edinburgh Reporter has given a two-star review to a production of 1984. The headline is all I have, so I can't tell you which production or edition it was, nor why it fell short. Even so, a lukewarm review of Orwell can be used in class: what would a good staging of that novel need to achieve, and why might it be so hard? Separately, Secret Miami reports that a long-running literary festival in Miami this November is featuring some five hundred authors, among them Margaret Atwood, Colson Whitehead and Tony Shalhoub. Atwood's The Handmaid's Tale is on your oral list, so if her appearance is recorded or written up, it could be good listening or reading material. I'd keep an eye out for it.

Closer to home, Place Gre'net has an archive page tagged with the Cité scolaire internationale in Grenoble. I only have the title, so I can't say what it covers, but it could be worth a look for local context on the school world you work in.

Now, a handful of pieces for pleasure rather than for the syllabus. RUSSPAIN.com carries a recommendation from Julia Otero of Ousman Umar's memoir about migration. I don't have details of the book, but a first-person account of a journey is the kind of narrator-led story you tend to enjoy, and it might sit interestingly beside the voices in Brick Lane. The Economist has an article asking why Max Richter's compositions have become so popular. Again I have only the headline, but Richter is an apt subject for someone who loves classical music and how it reaches new audiences. If you have the time, the question is a good one to carry into the next concert.

For something gothic, The Polytechnic, a student publication, runs an opinion piece titled Till Death Do Us Part, offering an interpretation of The Haunting of Hill House. From the title, it seems to read the story through marriage and mortality. I can't say more than that, but a student argument may be a nice example of close reading to show older pupils. In the world of dance, the Toowoomba Chronicle reports on a new three-year deal that will bring ballet to Toowoomba, in Australia. It's a small piece of good news about live performance reaching a regional town, and I rather like that. And last, The Hindu's books newsletter has a piece revisiting literary history. I only have the title, but it fits your fondness for the way novels and poems carry the past with them.

That's the round-up, Yamuna, and I hope the day gives you a few unhurried moments with a good book.
bfi.long:
Good morning, Yamuna. It's a quieter couple of days for the BFI, with no official texts or reforms to report, but a good handful of stagings and bits of literary news that touch the programme, so let me take them by theme.

Let me begin with Hamlet, which turns up three times and is clearly having a moment. The play is on the session 2027 list, so your première classes will be meeting it this year. First, Country and Town House has a stage note on Hamlet: Hail to the Thief at the Barbican in London. I should be frank that all I have is the headline, so I can't tell you how the production is staged, who is in it, or what the critic made of it. But the title suggests a version that sets the play in a particular light, and the Barbican is a significant venue, so it's worth a look if you want to see how a theatre is currently framing the play.

Second, there is a production at the Nevada Theatre in California, reported by TheUnion.com under the headline "A Hamlet for our time". It runs through the eighth of November, so only a matter of days remain, and it is a long way from Les Adrets. But the angle is useful in itself. Describing a Hamlet as being for our time is an old habit of theatre criticism, and it could make a nice small exercise with a class. What exactly makes a play written four centuries ago feel contemporary? Is it the politics, the surveillance, the grief, the young man who cannot act? Students can argue for their own answer using the text, and then see how far a production's claim holds up.

Third, BroadwayWorld announces that Thinking Cap Theatre is presenting Hamlet. Again it's only a headline, with no dates or details. I mention it mostly to show that the play is being staged in several places at once, which is handy for you. If any of your students have access to a local production, or a recording, the same speech performed by different companies is among the best ways to show that a text is not a fixed thing. Even without the productions, a comparison of two filmed or described versions of "To be or not to be" would make a good short lesson for première.

Staying with the stage, there are two items on other texts from the 2027 list. The first is a review of Great Expectations at the Brockley Jack Studio in south London, from southlondon.co.uk. Once more I have only the title, so I can't say how the adaptation handles Pip's narration, or Miss Havisham, or the marshes. What I can say is that a studio theatre staging of a Dickens novel is bound to make choices about compression, and those choices are exactly what a seconde or première class could discuss. What has to go when a novel of that length becomes an evening in a small room? Which scenes would your students refuse to cut? That sort of question gets them thinking about what is essential in the book, which is half the work of an essay.

The second is Patch reporting that tickets are now on sale for a Chatham High School staging of Twelfth Night. There is no date or venue in what I have, so it's a modest item, but I like it all the same. Twelfth Night is on the 2027 list, and it is a reminder that this play is very often a school play, which suits its comedy of disguise and mistaken identity. If you ever want your students to perform a scene rather than only analyse it, a school production on the other side of the Atlantic is a nice, friendly example to mention.

Alongside these, there's a piece of news that isn't tied to the programme but may please the theatre-lover in you. Shakespeare's Globe has released a video about a new play, The Animals Come to the Table, by Timberlake Wertenbaker. It will run at the Sam Wanamaker Playhouse from the eleventh of December twenty twenty-six to the twenty-fourth of January twenty twenty-seven. In the video, Wertenbaker talks with the director Anthony Lau about the work. I don't have any description of the plot beyond the title, so I won't guess. But a conversation between a playwright and a director is just the kind of thing you can sometimes use in class, to show students that a text is shaped by choices on both sides. And the Playhouse, with its candlelit indoor setting, is a venue many of your students might love to hear about, even if they can't go.

Now to the oral themes. The Edinburgh Reporter has given a two-star review to 1984. The text is only the headline, so I can't tell you whether it is a stage adaptation, a new edition, or something else, and I wouldn't like to guess. A two-star review is interesting in itself, though. Orwell's novel is on the oral list, and students are often a bit too reverent about canonical works. A negative review of a version of 1984 might be a good way to encourage them to be critical readers. What would a disappointing adaptation of this book look like? What do they think it must get right? That turns a bad review into a way of defining what matters in the novel.

There is also literary-festival news from Miami. Secret Miami reports that the country's longest-running literary festival is taking place this November, with around five hundred authors, among them Margaret Atwood, Colson Whitehead and Tony Shalhoub. Atwood's The Handmaid's Tale is on your oral list. The report is brief, so I don't know what she'll be speaking about, but if recordings or write-ups of her appearance emerge, they could be a good source of a living author's voice to set beside the text. Hearing an author talk, even briefly, tends to make a novel feel less like a set book and more like something someone chose to write.

On a local note, Place Gre'net has an article tagged under the Cité scolaire internationale in Grenoble, which is your own neighbourhood in a professional sense. I only have the archive title, so I can't tell you what it covers. If it touches on the life of the international sections, it could be a useful bit of context, and perhaps a reminder of how your school looks from the outside. I'd suggest a quick look when you have a moment.

Beyond the programme, there are a few items that may appeal to you as a reader rather than as a teacher. Julia Otero, writing on RUSSPAIN.com, recommends Ousman Umar's memoir about migration. Again I only have the headline, so I can't describe the book. But a first-person account of migration is, almost by definition, a story with a strong narrator, and that is something you've said you value. It could also sit usefully beside some of the novels you teach. Brick Lane, on the 2027 list, deals with displacement and belonging, and a memoir might offer a different angle on similar questions, though I'd want to read it before suggesting anything firm.

For gothic taste, there's a student opinion piece in The Polytechnic called "Till Death do us part", an interpretation of The Haunting of Hill House. The title suggests a reading around marriage and mortality, but the text I have is brief, so the argument itself isn't clear. It is not a professional review, just a student's reading, which makes it a small example of what your own students might produce. If you ever teach gothic elements in Great Expectations, with Miss Havisham and her stopped clocks and her decaying wedding dress, a reading that links marriage and death is rather apt. That is my own connection, not the article's, so take it as an idea rather than a report.

The Hindu's books newsletter also has a piece revisiting literary history. The text I have is only the title, so I can't say which period or which writers it looks back on. I mention it because you like novels that teach history, and a newsletter that returns to literary history may give you something to dip into over a coffee.

Finally, two items on music and dance, which are rather outside the BFI but, I think, within your taste. The Economist has an article exploring why Max Richter's compositions have become so popular. All I have is the headline, so I can't give you the argument. But a piece trying to explain why a contemporary composer reaches so many listeners is the sort of thing that might interest someone who loves classical music documentaries. And the Toowoomba Chronicle reports on a new three-year deal that will bring ballet to Toowoomba, in Australia. It is a good-news story about live performance reaching a regional town, and the three-year span suggests a real commitment rather than a one-off visit. It doesn't connect to the programme at all, but it is the sort of thing that is nice to know about.

So, to gather the practical points together. For première, the most useful thread this week is Hamlet, with three productions at three different venues. You could have students compare how the play is framed in each, using just the descriptions available, and then test those framings against the text. For Dickens and Shakespeare more generally, the stagings of Great Expectations and Twelfth Night offer an easy way into the question of adaptation, what gets kept and what gets lost. For the oral, the two-star 1984 review and the Atwood festival appearance each give you a way to bring a living, critical voice into the room. And I should repeat that most of these items were headlines only, so before you build a lesson on any of them, it would be worth opening the original to see what it actually says.

That's the corner for today, Yamuna, and I hope something here catches your eye over your morning coffee.

Good morning, Yamuna. This week's gentle pull is towards Friday evening and the weekend, with plenty happening in the Grésivaudan, a few good things in Meylan and Crolles, and a bit of news from your own village.

Let me begin with Friday, the sixth of November, because the valley is unusually busy that evening, and you may find yourself with a pleasant problem of choice.

The one I would put first, given how much you love a strong narrative voice, is Contes Shipibos by Compagnie Caminos. It takes place at Espace Aragon in Villard-Bonnot, starting at seven in the evening. It is an evening of Shipibo storytelling in the oral tradition, so there is no stage set to speak of and no screen, just tales told aloud across cultures. As a teacher of literature you will know that a story told by a living voice does something different from the same story on the page. The rhythm belongs to the teller, and the pauses are chosen in the moment. If you have ever wanted an evening that reminds you why narrators matter, this looks like a good candidate. Villard-Bonnot is a short drive along the valley, so it is an easy outing.

Later the same evening, in Pontcharra, there is a concert built around the songs of Anne Sylvestre. It runs from eight o'clock until twenty past nine, so it is a comfortable length, not a marathon. The listing describes it as French chanson with a strong literary streak, and that seems to me the right way to think of her work, as songs that care about words. If you enjoy passages that are beautiful as language, this is a way to meet that pleasure through music rather than through the page. It would also be a nice thing to mention to your older pupils, who may know little of the chanson tradition, as a living form of poetry set to melody.

Also in Pontcharra that same Friday there is a performance called AMOURS, by Cie Muchmuche Company, part of the Saison Echos season. I should be honest that the listing does not say what form it takes or what it contains, and it gives no start time in what I have. So it is more of a curiosity than a recommendation. If the title intrigues you, a quick look at the Saison Echos programme would tell you more. I mention it mainly because it means Pontcharra has two separate offerings that evening, which is rather lovely for a small town.

And there is a fourth option on the sixth, a concert by the Péninsule Trio at the Salle des fêtes Dupanloup in La Combe-de-Lancey. Again the listing does not state the programme or the genre, so I cannot tell you whether to expect jazz, classical or something in between. But a trio in a village hall is often an intimate, unfussy sort of concert, the kind where you can hear every note, and La Combe-de-Lancey is up in the hills of Belledonne, so it may even be one of the closest of the four to Les Adrets. If you like the idea of a village hall, a small ensemble and a quiet drive home, it may be worth finding out more.

So, four evenings in one, and you can only be in one place. If it were my choice, I would weigh up the storytelling against the songs of Anne Sylvestre, since both speak to the things you love most, voice and language. But the trio is a charming wildcard.

On Saturday, the seventh of November, there is another opening to note. At Saint-Maximin, the cultural season of Itinéraire bis begins. Le Dauphiné Libéré reports that the season starts that day. The paper's piece gives no programme in what I have, but a season opening is often a good moment to look at the whole calendar, pick out a few evenings and book ahead. Saint-Maximin sits conveniently between the Grésivaudan and Grenoble, so it is within easy reach for concerts or performances over the coming weeks. If you like discovering a small venue that is not on every list, this is a good one to keep an eye on.

Now, for the weekend as a whole, from Friday the sixth to Sunday the eighth, two outlets have published round-ups that may save you some searching. The first is jds.fr, which has a piece on what is on in Isère that weekend. It mentions concerts, the Foire de Grenoble, shows and what it calls unusual activities. The second is ici.fr, which has a similar round-up of ideas for outings across Isère over the long weekend. That one is brief, but it points to a good range of options. I do not have the details from either, so I cannot tell you what the unusual activities are. But if you want a Saturday with no fixed plan, those two pages are a sensible place to begin. The Foire de Grenoble is the big name in the list, and it is the sort of thing that either appeals or does not, so I will leave that to your mood.

Let me turn from the weekend to the month. Le Dauphiné Libéré has a preview saying that Pontcharra will host many cultural events in November. The article, at least as I have it, does not give a programme, so I cannot name them. But taken together with the two Friday offerings I mentioned, it does suggest the town is having a busy cultural season. If Pontcharra is convenient for you, it might be worth looking at the town's own listings and seeing what else is coming. The Friday concert and the AMOURS performance look like the first of several.

Then there is news from home. Les Adrets is to hold its Fête d'automne for the fifty-fourth time. Le Dauphiné Libéré reports the return of the festival, but the text I have gives no dates, so I cannot tell you when it falls. I can only say that fifty-four editions is a long tradition for a village of our size, and it is the sort of warm, local celebration that is rather lovely to attend on foot, without needing to plan a drive. If you do not already know the date, the mairie or the village noticeboards will almost certainly have it. And since you love producers' markets and village life, I suspect this one will feel very much like your sort of occasion.

Moving to exhibitions, there are two to mention, and neither asks much of your time. In Crolles, from the fourth of November until the fourth of December, there is a photography exhibition called Brayogrammes by Cédric Poulain. Entry is free, and it runs for a full month, so you can fit it around a market morning or a trip to the valley without any pressure. I do not have a description of the images themselves, so I cannot tell you what to expect, but a free month-long exhibition of photography is an easy thing to say yes to. Given your interest in the link between images and written work, it could be a nice excuse to look at pictures with a narrator's eye, asking what story each frame is telling.

In Grenoble, from the third to the thirtieth of November, there is a month of accessibility-themed activities, all free. The details are thin, and I cannot tell you what the activities include, but it is a broad local calendar item and may offer something interesting through the month. I mention it more as a pointer than a recommendation, so you can look it up if the theme interests you, or perhaps if it is relevant to your work with pupils.

Now to the theatre at Meylan. The Théâtre Hexagone, the scène nationale, has three pieces in the listings, and they could hardly be more different from one another.

The first has already begun. SOIF, by Bougier TOTO, was staged on Wednesday evening, the fourth of November, at eight o'clock, and runs for about one hour twenty. It explores belief within contemporary knowledge, and water and memory. The listing says one further date is given, though I do not have it, so it is worth checking the Hexagone's website if the themes appeal. Water and memory are such rich images for literature, so I would be tempted by it.

Next comes something much heavier. On Wednesday the eighteenth of November, at ten in the morning, the Hexagone presents Azaline se tait, by Les Veilleurs, for ages ten and up, running about one hour ten. It follows a child confined to night and the need to speak out about incest. Three more dates are listed. I want to be careful here, because the subject is difficult, and the morning time suggests it may be aimed partly at school groups. It is serious theatre, and for a reader who wants that, it may be valuable. But it is not an evening to go into lightly, and you might want to read the company's own notes beforehand to know what to expect.

Finally, something lighter. On Wednesday the twenty-fifth of November, at half past seven in the evening, the Hexagone hosts Le Poids des choses, a circus and illusion show by Camille Boitel, for ages seven and up, lasting about forty-five minutes. It plays with gravity, and two more dates are listed. I like the sound of it for you because it is physical and playful, and you enjoy dance documentaries, so you might enjoy watching bodies and objects negotiate with weight. At forty-five minutes, it is also a lovely short evening, with time left over for supper afterwards.

One last item, and I will keep it brief since cinema is not your main interest. Grenoble is hosting the twentieth edition of the Dolce Cinema festival, which is dedicated to Italian cinema, according to jds.fr. The date is not given in what I have, so I cannot say when it falls. But if Italian films, and the strong storytelling that often comes with them, tempt you, it is a milestone edition and worth looking up.

So, to gather it all together. This Friday offers storytelling in Villard-Bonnot, Anne Sylvestre's songs in Pontcharra, a mystery performance in the same town, and a trio concert in La Combe-de-Lancey. Saturday brings the opening of the Itinéraire bis season in Saint-Maximin. The weekend round-ups from jds.fr and ici.fr can help fill in the gaps. Photography in Crolles and a month of accessibility activities in Grenoble are there whenever you have a spare hour. Meylan has three very different pieces through November. And back in Les Adrets, the fifty-fourth Fête d'automne is on its way, so it is worth watching for the date.

I hope one of these finds its way into your week, Yamuna, and that the mountain air makes the drive home as pleasant as the evening itself.

good.short:
Good morning, Yamuna. Today's good news has a decidedly literary bent, with prizes, buried histories and a few small miracles from the natural world.

Let me begin with books, since the past two days have been generous to them. On Tuesday, Philippe Jaenada, aged sixty-two, won the Prix Goncourt for L'Inconnue du quai de Javel. Franceinfo reports that on France Inter he spoke of joy and emotion, and said it felt like a kind of vertigo. The Guardian describes the book as a literary investigation into the murder, in nineteen forty-nine, of Louise Cansot, a Breton woman who worked as a life model in Paris. Jaenada tries to solve a case now seventy-seven years old, and to restore the reputation of the victim. For someone who likes history taught through fiction, that sounds like a book to put on the list, perhaps even for a première class curious about how a novelist can act as detective and advocate at once.

Another prize, this time for poetry. Grace Nichols, the Guyana-born, British-based poet, has won the ten thousand pound Royal Society of Literature Pioneer prize, which honours women writers over sixty who broke barriers. The Guardian quotes her being called a trailblazer in the truest sense. She is best known for I Is a Long-Memoried Woman, a title that is itself a small piece of music. And on the dance side, the Guardian has an interview with the Greek choreographer Christos Papadopoulos, winner of the first Rose international prize for choreography, which some are calling the Turner prize for dance. He won it for Larsen C, and he talks candidly about failure, friction, and asking the near-impossible of dancers. It is a good read if you enjoy hearing artists describe how they work.

Now to stories from the past that read like novels. The Beaux Arts Magazine reports that the château de Chantilly is exploring the fate of its pink diamond, stolen in nineteen twenty-six, later recovered, and wrapped ever since in legend. One of the curators calls it a miracle survivor. Theft, disappearance and rediscovery in a single jewel is rather hard to beat as a plot.

Then there is a story from Upworthy that deserves a slow telling. During the Second World War, the maharaja Digvijaysinhji Ranjitsinhji Jadeja took in around one thousand Polish children and recreated a home for them on Indian soil. Think of what that means: children far from everything they knew, given somewhere to belong. It is a story of rescue and identity that a novelist could hardly improve upon.

Good News Network offers two more along those lines. The first is a short documentary from JoyDrops called The Grandfather Puzzle. The filmmaker Ora DeKornfeld pieces together the hidden family history of her grandfather, a man who would not speak of it, after he turned ninety-nine. It has that shape you enjoy, of a buried past slowly coming up into the light. The second is from Punjab, where Sikhs and Hindus are organising the rebuilding of old mosques that were destroyed after Partition, while Muslims look on. The effort is led largely by people who remember the violence themselves, which makes it a very moving act of repair, and a reminder that memory can build as well as wound.

Staying with the past, and with music: Good News Network notes that today, the fifth of November, is the anniversary of the reopening of the Vienna State Opera in nineteen fifty-five, after its destruction in the Second World War. It is a house tied to Mahler and to the Vienna Philharmonic, so you may like to listen to something from that tradition this evening, in honour of a building that was rebuilt.

On to nature, where there is plenty of encouragement. The Optimist Daily reports that researchers at Stanford have found that bleached coral can heal through touch. A bleached fragment began to recover within days after being placed against a healthy one, which passed along the symbiotic algae the bleached coral had lost. It is a small, concrete finding, and one that offers real hope for reefs.

From Scotland, Good News Network says beavers are set to return to the Loch Ness area after about five hundred years. They were last recorded there between fifteen twenty-six and fifteen twenty-seven. They are described as ecosystem engineers, shaping the land and water for countless other creatures, so Loch Ness is about to get a new sort of monster, and a rather useful one.

The Optimist Daily also has a profile of Maya Higa, part of its Local Changemakers series for twenty twenty-six. She built a wildlife sanctuary on Twitch, funded by the people who watch it. The piece opens with her refusing to swim with sperm whales in Dominica, which is a wonderful way to begin a story about conservation, and it sets the tone for someone who puts the animals' interests first.

And if the sky is clear, there is something to look forward to. The new moon falls on Monday the ninth of November, which should make the night sky especially dark. The Northern Taurid meteor shower is due to peak a few days after that, and the darkness should help you see its long, luminous tails. From Les Adrets, with the valley lights well below you, it could be a lovely thing to step outside for.

Last, two items about the way people live together. Positive News describes a village in England that has set up a social care community based on shared living and shared responsibility, rather than on care as a conventional service. The article asks whether the idea could spread, and it is a thoughtful piece about how we look after one another. Closer to home, Le Dauphiné Libéré says Pontcharra will host many cultural events this November. The preview gives no programme, but it is a useful lead for a Grésivaudan weekend, so it may be worth a look at the town's listings.

That is all for today, and I hope the diamond, the beavers and the meteors keep you good company until tomorrow.
good.long:
Good morning, Yamuna. Today's good news arrives in a loose, pleasant order: prizes for people who write and move beautifully, old stories of rescue and repair, and a few small, hopeful victories in the natural world.

Let me begin with books, since the week has been generous to them. On Tuesday, Philippe Jaenada, aged sixty-two, won the Prix Goncourt for L'Inconnue du quai de Javel. Franceinfo reports that he spoke on France Inter about the news, and the word he reached for was vertigo. He described a feeling of joy and emotion, the sort of dizzy happiness that comes when something you have worked on quietly for years is suddenly held up in public. It is nice to hear a writer sound a little unsteady with delight rather than rehearsed.

The Guardian gives us more about the book itself, and it is the kind of subject I think you will enjoy. It calls it a true crime novel, or more precisely a literary investigation, into the murder in nineteen forty-nine of Louise Cansot, a Breton woman who worked in Paris as a life model. The case is now seventy-seven years old. Jaenada sets out to solve it, but also to restore the reputation of the victim, who, as the paper's account suggests, had been treated unfairly in the telling. So here is a book that is part thriller, part history, part act of justice done on the page, and it has just been given France's biggest literary prize. It is also a reminder of something you already know well: that a novel can teach a period, here postwar Paris, with more texture than any textbook manages. If you are looking for something to read over the autumn, with a victim whose name is finally being said with respect, this may be it.

Staying with writers, The Guardian also reports that Grace Nichols has won the Royal Society of Literature's Pioneer prize, worth ten thousand pounds. Nichols was born in Guyana and is based in Britain, and she is best known for I Is a Long-Memoried Woman. The prize honours women writers over sixty who have broken barriers, and the paper quotes a tribute calling her a trailblazer in the truest sense. I like the shape of this prize, because it recognises that some writers do their pioneering work long before the world catches up, and it says so without hurry. I Is a Long-Memoried Woman is a fine thing to put in front of older pupils, I would think: a voice with rhythm and memory in it, and a history carried in the sound of the language rather than only in its subject matter.

From the writing of history to the history itself, there is a handful of stories this week about rescue, mystery and repair. The first is a glittering one. Beaux Arts Magazine tells us that the château de Chantilly is exploring the fate of its pink diamond, which was stolen in nineteen twenty-six, later recovered, and has been wrapped in legend ever since. One of the people quoted calls the diamond a miraculé, a survivor against the odds. Theft, disappearance, rediscovery, a stone that seems to have refused to stay lost: it reads like the opening chapters of a novel, and I suspect it would make a very good starting point for a creative writing exercise. Who steals a diamond? Who keeps the secret? Chantilly is not far to travel in spirit, even if it is a little far in practice, but it is the sort of exhibition story that belongs on your list.

The second story of rescue is, I think, one of the most moving of the week. Upworthy tells of the maharaja Digvijaysinhji Ranjitsinhji Jadeja, who during the Second World War took in around one thousand Polish children and recreated a home for them on Indian soil. Think about that for a moment. Children who had lost their country, arriving in a place that was entirely foreign to them, and a ruler deciding that what they needed was not merely shelter but a sense of home, a place that would still feel like Poland. It is a story about identity as much as safety, about how a language, a routine, and a familiar table can hold a child together. It is also history that could easily be read as a novel, with its wide cast of children and its unlikely benefactor. For a classroom, it speaks to the idea that stories can be entered without prior knowledge of the culture, because the feelings are so plainly human.

The third comes from Punjab, and it is a quieter, more tender piece of repair. Good News Network reports that Sikhs and Hindus there are organising the rebuilding of old mosques that were destroyed after Partition, while Muslims look on. What strikes me is who is leading it: largely people who remember the violence. Those who lived through the destruction are the ones choosing to rebuild, and I find that profoundly hopeful. It is not an abstract gesture of reconciliation, but bricks, mortar and memory. Partition has given the English-language canon some of its most powerful novels, and here is a real-life chapter that might belong at the end of one of them, in which the survivors, long afterwards, decide to put something back.

The last in this group is a small film. Good News Network highlights The Grandfather Puzzle, a short documentary from JoyDrops, in which the filmmaker Ora DeKornfeld pieces together the hidden family history of her grandfather after he turned ninety-nine. He had long declined to talk about it. There is something very novelistic in that set-up: an elderly man, a buried past, a granddaughter with a camera and a great deal of patience. It speaks to the way families keep their stories, and how late in life they sometimes allow them out. If you have an evening free and want something short and humane, this might suit.

Now to music and dance, which you know I have not forgotten. Good News Network's history column reminds us that on the fifth of November, nineteen fifty-five, the Vienna State Opera reopened after being destroyed in the Second World War. The note links the house to Mahler and the Vienna Philharmonic. There is something lovely about the date, a building coming back to life a decade after the war, and with it a whole musical tradition that had been interrupted. It is a good day to put on a Mahler symphony, if you were looking for an excuse, and the story offers a tidy lesson for pupils too: that culture is among the first things we rebuild when we can.

On the dance side, The Guardian has an interview with the Greek choreographer Christos Papadopoulos, who has won the first Rose international prize for choreography, which the paper nicknames the Turner prize for dance. He won it for his piece Larsen C. In the conversation he talks about failure and friction, and about asking the near-impossible of his dancers, and he also reflects on what the prize money means to him. I like this because it is honest about the craft: the idea that good work often comes out of difficulty, and that the people doing the dancing are being pushed to the edge of what a body can do. If you ever want to show your sixth-formers how an artist thinks about risk, this interview would be a good companion piece.

Let me turn now to the natural world, where there is some genuinely encouraging science. The Optimist Daily reports that researchers at Stanford have found that bleached coral can heal through touch. A fragment of bleached coral began to recover within days after being placed against a healthy one, which passed along the symbiotic algae the bleached piece had lost. Coral bleaching is usually reported as a loss, so a result which is concrete, observed and quick is quietly thrilling. It is only one finding, and I would not want to overstate it, but it points to a kind of mutual aid in the sea that nobody was counting on.

Further north, Good News Network says beavers are set to return to the area around Loch Ness after about five hundred years. The last recorded presence there was between fifteen twenty-six and fifteen twenty-seven. The piece describes them as ecosystem engineers, animals that reshape water and land in ways that help many other creatures, and it has a light, almost mischievous tone, welcoming a new monster to the loch. I rather like the idea that the real monster of Loch Ness turns out to be a rodent with a talent for dams, and that after half a millennium it is coming home.

There is a human-and-animal story too. The Optimist Daily profiles Maya Higa as part of its Local Changemakers 2026 series. She built a wildlife sanctuary on Twitch, funded by the people who watch it. The piece opens with her refusal to swim with sperm whales in Dominica, which is a memorable beginning, because it tells you immediately that her idea of loving wildlife is about leaving it alone rather than getting close for the sake of a photograph. Whatever one thinks of streaming, it is a good example of an audience being turned into a community that pays for something concrete. Your older pupils may well know the platform better than you or I do, and it might make a good talking point about where good can come from online.

And for something you can do yourself, Good News Network points to the Northern Taurid meteor shower. The New Moon falls on Monday the ninth of November, which should make the sky as dark as it gets, and the shower is due to peak a few days after that. The Taurids are known for long, luminous tails. From Les Adrets, with Belledonne at your back and the valley lights below, you are about as well placed as anyone could be, as long as the clouds co-operate. Wrap up warmly and give your eyes a little time to adjust.

Two last items, both about people and place. Positive News asks what would happen if we stopped treating social care as a service, and looks at a village in England that has set up a social care community built on communal living and shared responsibility. The question the piece poses is whether the model could spread. It is a thoughtful read about how people look after one another, and it is not hard to see the novel in it: a village, a set of neighbours, the ordinary dramas of caring and being cared for.

And closer to home, Le Dauphiné Libéré says that Pontcharra will host many cultural events this November. The preview does not give the programme, so I can't tell you what to book, but for someone in the Grésivaudan it is a good lead to follow up. A quick look at the town's listings this week might turn up a concert or an exhibition worth the short drive down from the mountain.

That is the lot for today, Yamuna, so enjoy your coffee, and perhaps keep one eye on the night sky next week.

Good morning, Yamuna. It's Thursday the fifth of November, and over the last two days France has given us a new Goncourt winner, some restless lycées, a returning gentleman thief and a handful of nice little language lessons.

Let me start with the book news, since it's the best of it. The Prix Goncourt was awarded on Tuesday to Philippe Jaenada, who is sixty-two, for his book L'Inconnue du quai de Javel. Franceinfo caught his reaction on France Inter, where he spoke of joy and emotion, and the headline borrows his own words: "Ça ressemble vraiment à un vertige". It really feels like vertigo, he said, which is a rather lovely thing for a writer to say when handed the country's biggest literary prize.

The Guardian describes the book as a true crime novel, and as a literary investigation. It looks into the murder, in nineteen forty-nine, of a woman called Louise Cansot. She was Breton, and she worked in Paris as a life model, so she is someone who spent her working days being looked at, and, it seems, rarely listened to. The case is now seventy-seven years old, and the book sets out to solve it. Just as important, according to the Guardian, it sets out to restore her reputation. That's a fascinating double ambition: part detective story, part act of repair. For someone who likes history taught through fiction, and who has a soft spot for a thriller with a conscience, it sounds like one to put on the list. There's also a pleasing link to the world of painting that you might enjoy, a young woman whose profession was to pose for artists, and who is finally given a voice by a writer. I'd only add that this is my own reflection on the premise, and I haven't seen anything yet on how the book handles it.

Jaenada also turns up in the other corner of today's material, which is the daily television roundup from La Mire. I'll come back to that in a moment.

Now to schools, which I know sits close to home for you. There are two stories here, and they fit together. On Tuesday the third of November, students blockaded dozens of high schools and universities across France. The Local France reports that they were rejecting proposed government education reforms. The same report notes that turnout was lower than on earlier blockade days, so the movement may be losing a little steam, though that's a cautious reading and I wouldn't lean on it too heavily.

Franceinfo, meanwhile, looks at the consequences. Lycée blockades carried on on Monday, which was the first day back after the Toussaint holidays, even though the government had made announcements meant to calm things down. The education minister, Edouard Geffray, says the school year is at risk for several hundred thousand pupils. Headteachers are worried about delays building up ahead of the baccalauréat. The franceinfo headline puts it very plainly, with a quotation: "On ne pourra pas tout rattraper". We won't be able to catch everything up. It's a sober phrase, and it will ring true for anyone who has ever tried to recover a lost fortnight in a syllabus. Since you teach seconde and première, and have terminale ahead of you with the BFI, you'll know better than I do how much that matters in practice. I'll simply say that the question now is whether the disruption fades, or whether it begins to bite into teaching time before the exams.

If you want the television view of all this, La Mire's video for Tuesday the third of November is a quick way in. It's their daily look at what French channels are reporting, and that day it covered the school blockades, a presidential hopeful, cyberattacks and artificial intelligence. Some of that is politics, so you can dip in for the school segment and leave the rest.

The Wednesday edition, for the fourth of November, is a zapping across channels including Arte and France 5. There are political segments in it that you may well want to skip, but it also includes an item on the Glacier Blanc, one of the giants of the French Alps. That's close to your own mountains, so it may be worth a look. And it features Philippe Jaenada as the new Goncourt winner, so you'd get to see him on screen as well.

On to lighter things. There's a good clutch of entertainment stories this morning, and the first is for thriller lovers. Netflix's Lupin is back for a fourth season, with Omar Sy once again as the gentleman thief. The Guardian's reviewer is thoroughly won over. They call him ridiculously watchable and effortlessly charming, and a blindingly brilliant thief, and they praise the twisty writing and the ensemble cast around him. Lupin is, of course, a character born in fiction, Maurice Leblanc's creation, so there's a literary lineage here for the lycée if you ever want a way into French popular fiction. The review is simply about the series, though, so I'll leave the literary pedigree as my own aside.

Two much-loved comic-book heroes are also having birthdays. Franceinfo reports that Lucky Luke, the cowboy who shoots faster than his own shadow, is celebrating his eightieth anniversary, and is, as the title says, still in fine form. The piece also notes that Blake and Mortimer turn eighty this year as well. So two very different bande dessinée worlds, one a sunlit Western, the other a more shadowy British adventure, have been going for the same eight decades. It's a gentle reminder of how deeply the bande dessinée sits in French culture, and how many generations have grown up with these characters.

And the warmest story of the lot comes from the Guardian. It's a profile of Philippe Peythieu and Véronique Augereau, who have been the French voices of Homer and Marge Simpson for thirty-eight years. They fell in love while working on the show, and they are now married in real life. In the interview they talk about what it's like to work together and live together, and how they've stayed close. There's something rather delightful about a couple who spend their working days as one of television's most famous marriages, and who turn out to have a real one that works. If you want a story to start the day with a smile, this is the one.

Now a small corner for words, which I suspect you'll like. The Local France has two of its French Expressions of the Day. The first is "être à couteaux tirés", literally to be at drawn knives. The press uses it when relations between people or groups are hostile, which is vivid enough that you hardly need a dictionary. The second is "faire amende honorable". The piece points out that this has nothing to do with the word "amende" meaning a fine, which is a nice trap for English speakers and French learners alike. It's a tidy example of how a word can look as if it explains an idiom and in fact does nothing of the kind. Both pieces are short, and both could do very well as a warm-up with a class that likes etymology.

The Local's podcast this week also has a language segment, asking which city locals consider to speak the purest, the most "perfect", French. It's the sort of question that starts friendly arguments at dinner tables. The same episode touches on the latest on French protests, with a tear gas warning, and on a possible easing of doctors' appointments in rural France. That second item may interest you as someone living in the hills, since access to doctors is a real matter in countryside areas, though the summary I have doesn't go into detail, and doesn't say anything specific about the Alps or Isère.

On practical life, there are two items. First, the French telecoms regulator has published detailed new maps showing how good phone and internet coverage is across the country, and The Local France has written them up. If you've ever lost a signal on the road up to Les Adrets, you may be curious. I should be honest that the piece I have gives no local figures, so I can't tell you what the maps say about Belledonne or the Grésivaudan. It may just be worth a look for yourself when you have a moment.

Second, a hint of good news for anyone who travels with animals. The Local France reports that an agreement between the EU and the UK, expected at the upcoming summit, could bring back pet passports. That would make Channel crossings easier for holidaymakers travelling with dogs, cats and ferrets. The deal hasn't been announced yet, so for now it's a prospect rather than a settled change, and it's worth watching rather than planning around. Still, anyone who has dealt with the paperwork for a pet crossing the Channel will understand why this is welcome news.

And finally, one human-interest video from HugoDécrypte, published on the third of November, about a man who says he walked around the world on foot over twenty-eight years. The summary gives no further detail, so I can't tell you where he went or why. But a journey that long is a story in itself, and it might be a pleasant thing to watch with a cup of tea, perhaps with a certain curiosity about what twenty-eight years of walking does to a person's view of the world.

So that's the shape of things this morning: a murdered life model given her story back, schools holding their breath before the bac, a thief with a charming smile, two cartoon veterans at eighty, and a pair of idioms to play with.

Enjoy your Thursday, Yamuna, and may your signal hold all the way up the hill.
