Good morning, Yamuna. It's a rich couple of days on Arte in particular, with some good thrillers, a fair amount of history told like fiction, and a few musical anniversaries to mark.

Let me start with the thrillers, since one of them is on tonight. Arte is showing Anatomie d'un instant this evening, Thursday the fifth of November. It's a series that dramatises the moment Spain's history turned on a coup attempt. It's the kind of drama you like, where a historical hinge is explored through character and tension rather than through a lecture, and I can imagine it being a lovely thing to bring into a conversation with older pupils. Over on Netflix, ELLE says Keira Knightley and Sarah Lancashire return this week in a spy thriller it calls addictive, with the headline "Can't Look Away". CNET, meanwhile, has a piece on when new episodes arrive for the second season of Black Doves, which appears to be the very same series. If you want something to binge on a dark November evening, with two strong women at its centre, that looks like the one.

Now to the heavier side of Arte's schedule, where there's a pair of documentaries that read like thrillers but are very much real history. Criminel nazi cherche employeur follows Walther Rauff, the former SS officer tied to the gas vans of the Final Solution. Part one traces him from the war to his peaceful death in Pinochet's Chile in nineteen eighty-four. Part two goes through the Chilean junta's detention island and the Colonia Dignidad, with a link to Pinochet. It's described as a gripping archival investigation, hard history told in the manner of a novel, so do watch the first part before the second. It is not light viewing, but it sounds compelling.

Also on Arte is Vivre en Ukraine, en guerre, a wordless, hypnotic documentary with wide shots of Kyiv, the front line and ordinary lives, including a statue of Soviet friendship being toppled. It's described as a quiet, unsparing portrait of a nation changed by war, and it's available until the tenth of December this year. Another piece, from Arte Regards, is a thirty-one-minute reportage from this year on the exhumation of infants and children buried at the Tuam mother-and-baby home in Ireland. Survivors and campaigners, among them Anna Corrigan and PJ Haverty, are seeking justice. It will be a sombre watch, and it's available until the third of November next year. And there's a retrospective on Jean Gabin, marking fifty years since his death on the fifteenth of November nineteen seventy-six. Rather than his films, it focuses on his wartime service with the Free French Forces from nineteen forty-three to nineteen forty-five. Its title translates as "war is not cinema", which rather sums up the angle.

Now something I think you might enjoy most, because it sits where literature and images meet. Arte has a documentary called Zola intime, naissance d'un photographe, about Émile Zola's late-life passion for photography, which began in eighteen eighty-eight at Royan. It links his writing to his documentary eye, so the way he looked at the world as a novelist meets the way he framed it through a lens. For anyone who loves the dialogue between paintings, pictures and prose, it sounds ideal, and perhaps a spark for a lesson on observation and realism.

For something a little different, Arte also has an episode of Voyages au pays des maths called Sur la route de l'infini. It explores infinity and Georg Cantor's set theory, which shows that infinity comes in different sizes. It's a strange and rather beautiful idea, almost poetic in itself, and the episode stays on replay until the fifth of April twenty twenty-eight, so there's no hurry.

On to music and dance, where the news is mostly in print this time. The Guardian marks the hundred-and-fiftieth anniversary of Brahms's First Symphony, which was premiered on the fourth of November eighteen seventy-six in Karlsruhe. It had taken him twenty-one years, beginning in the mid-eighteen-fifties, and the piece looks at how he wrestled with what he called a giant on his back, the weight of Beethoven's legacy. It's a good story about a creator paralysed by his predecessors, and then producing a masterpiece anyway. There is sadder news in the same pages: the conductor Herbert Blomstedt has died at the age of ninety-nine. The Guardian's obituary recalls a career of seven decades that took in the San Francisco Symphony and the Leipzig Gewandhaus. It's a tribute rather than good news, but a fitting one to read alongside the Brahms.

For opera, the Royal Opera has released a trailer for its production of Puccini's Tosca, directed by Oliver Mears. It stars Aleksandra Kurzak, Saimir Pirgu and Christopher Maltman, with Daniel Oren conducting. It's only a trailer, so a taste rather than the full performance, but Tosca is a proper operatic thriller, with love, police intrigue and a dreadful bargain, so it may well suit your taste. In Athens, meanwhile, the violinist and conductor Pinchas Zukerman is set to open the Athens International Music Festival. The report gives no further details beyond the announcement, but it's one to keep an eye on.

He won it for his piece Larsen C. He talks candidly about failure and friction, about asking the near-impossible of dancers, and about what the prize money means to him. It's a thoughtful read for anyone drawn to how art gets made.

That's everything for today, Yamuna, so choose a few, pour something warm, and enjoy the evening.

In the conversation he talks about failure, about friction, and about asking the near-impossible of dancers, and about what the prize money means to him. Given your love of dance documentaries, this is one to read with a coffee. A first-ever prize in a field often feels like a quiet moment of recognition, and the interview seems to be candid about how uneven the road there was.

One more piece of classical news, though a thin one. The violinist and conductor Pinchas Zukerman is set to open the Athens International Music Festival, according to tovima.com. The text gives no date and no programme, so all I can say is that it is an announcement, but it is a good name to open a festival with, and worth keeping an eye on if you are ever heading that way.

And finally, something a bit different, for the days when you want your mind stretched. Arte has an episode of Voyages au pays des maths called Sur la route de l'infini. It explores infinity and Georg Cantor's set theory, which shows that infinity comes in different sizes. That is one of those ideas that sounds like a paradox and turns out to be a rigorous argument, and it has a poetic quality that I think a literature teacher might enjoy: the idea that some endlessnesses are larger than others sounds like something out of Borges. It is on replay until the fifth of April, twenty twenty-eight, so there is no hurry at all.

So, to pull the threads together. If you want something live and gripping, Anatomie d'un instant is on Arte tonight. For a binge, Netflix has the return of the spy thriller. For serious history with a narrative drive, the two parts of the Walther Rauff documentary are the ones to start with, followed by the Gabin retrospective and the wordless portrait of Ukraine, with the Tuam reportage held back for a day when you are ready for it. Zola and the infinity episode are the gentler, more reflective pair, and the Brahms anniversary, the Tosca trailer and the Papadopoulos interview will carry the music and dance side of your week.

Enjoy the viewing, Yamuna, and may the evening bring you a good story and a warm cup of something.

briefing.text:
Good morning, Yamuna, and happy Thursday, the fifth of November.

Let's begin with books, and a rather wonderful question from The Guardian: was one of the great novels of the Enlightenment written by a man who believed he was a werewolf? The man is Jan Potocki, and the novel is The Manuscript Found in Saragossa, a surreal, nested, wandering book with a famously strange origin story. There's an exhibition devoted to it, and the curators argue that its global humanism feels especially relevant now. For someone who loves an unreliable narrator who keeps leading you down another path, it sounds like very good company.

Also on the book front, RNZ has gathered six experts to review the nominees for the twenty twenty-six Booker Prize, with critical judgements on each of the shortlisted novels. It's a handy way to arm yourself for the staffroom, or to find your next read. And from Literary Hub comes an opening passage of fiction called Remember the Bees. It is set on red earth, under an early and lingering heat, with a grandfather at its centre. The extract is brief, but the narration is sensory and quiet, the sort you can sink into over a coffee.

Now to art, where stories and objects meet. At the château de Chantilly, an exploration of the pink diamond is under way, and Beaux Arts Magazine calls it a miracle survivor. The jewel was stolen in nineteen twenty-six, later recovered, and has been wrapped in legend ever since. Theft, rediscovery, mystery: it reads like a novel before anyone has written the first line.

Closer to home, the Musée de Grenoble is showing sculptures and paintings by Anne Truitt. The listing from jds.fr is very short and gives no dates, so it's worth checking the museum's own information before you go. But it's your museum, and well worth keeping an eye on.

And on the screen, there's an ARTE documentary called Zola intime. It looks at Émile Zola's late-life passion for photography, which began in eighteen eighty-eight at Royan. It's a chance to see how his writer's documentary eye also worked through a lens, a lovely bridge between literature and image.

Staying with the screen, and with the stage, The Guardian has an interview with the Greek choreographer Christos Papadopoulos. He has won the first Rose international prize for choreography, which the paper nicknames the Turner Prize for dance, for his piece Larsen C. He talks about failure, about friction, and about asking the near-impossible of dancers, and about what the prize money means to him. One to read slowly, I think.

Now to your corner for the British section. A review has appeared on southlondon.co.uk of Great Expectations at the Brockley Jack Studio in London. All I have is the title, so I can't tell you what the review says, but with Dickens on the twenty twenty-seven session list, it may be worth a glance for staging ideas with seconde and première. And a little further ahead, Shakespeare's Globe will stage a new play by Timberlake Wertenbaker, The Animals Come to the Table, at the Sam Wanamaker Playhouse, from the eleventh of December to the twenty-fourth of January. There's a video in which the playwright and the director, Anthony Lau, talk about the work.

For some good news, today is an anniversary. On the fifth of November, nineteen fifty-five, the Vienna State Opera reopened after its destruction in the Second World War. Good News Network links the house to Mahler and the Vienna Philharmonic. It's worth pausing over the thought of a whole city deciding that music should come back first, or at least early.

And a second piece of good news, in a different key. Good News Network also features a short documentary in the JoyDrops series. The filmmaker Ora DeKornfeld pieces together her grandfather's hidden family history, after he turned ninety-nine and had never talked about it. A buried past, a patient granddaughter, and, one hopes, a good ending.

Now to the neighbourhood. For this weekend, the sixth to the eighth of November, jds.fr has a round-up for Isère: concerts, the Foire de Grenoble, shows, and a few unusual activities. It's a good place to start if you want to plan something close to Les Adrets. And in the Grésivaudan, Le Dauphiné Libéré says Pontcharra will host many cultural events this month. The preview gives no programme details, so it's a lead to follow up rather than a plan, but the valley may well surprise you.

One piece of school news, which you will want to know. Lycée blockades continued on Monday, the first day back after the Toussaint holidays, despite government announcements. According to franceinfo, the minister, Edouard Geffray, says the school year is at risk for several hundred thousand pupils, and headteachers are worried about delays before the bac. The line that caught my ear was, "on ne pourra pas tout rattraper": we won't be able to make up everything. It's worth keeping an eye on how it affects your seconde, première and terminale classes.

And to finish on words, The Local France has its French Expression of the Day: faire amende honorable. It means to make a public apology, and the piece notes that it has nothing to do with the word amende meaning a fine. A small treat for a teacher who likes to turn words over.

That's your Thursday, Yamuna; I hope the day treats you kindly, and that there's something beautiful to read at the end of it.
